claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from chromatin fractionation experiments showing enhanced STAT2 DNA binding in FLCN knockout cells.

claims.claim: FLCN loss slows cellular proliferation.
claims.source: Mechanistically, FLCN loss promotes STAT2 recruitment to chromatin and slows cellular proliferation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from growth curve measurements showing significantly reduced proliferation in FLCN knockout cells.

claims.claim: STAT1/2 signaling is a novel target of FLCN in renal cells and BHD tumors.
claims.source: Our integrated analysis identifies STAT1/2 signaling as a novel target of FLCN in renal cells and BHD tumors.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNAseq, proteomics, and analysis of BHD tumor samples showing upregulation of STAT1/2 and their target genes.

claims.claim: STAT1/2 activation appears to counterbalance TFE3-directed hyper-proliferation.
claims.source: STAT1/2 activation appears to counterbalance TFE3-directed hyper-proliferation and may influence immune responses.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations showing that FLCN loss reduces proliferation despite TFE3 activation, and that STAT1/2 knockdown partially rescues this phenotype.

claims.claim: STAT1/2 activation may influence immune responses.
claims.source: STAT1/2 activation appears to counterbalance TFE3-directed hyper-proliferation and may influence immune responses.
claims.evidence: This is speculative, based on the known role of STAT1/2 in immune responses and the observation of interferon response gene activation.

claims.claim: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common form of kidney cancer representing up to 5% of newly identified cancer cases.
claims.source: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common form of kidney cancer representing up to 5% of newly identified cancer cases (Ferlay et al., 2019; Lopez-Beltran et al., 2006; Siegel et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies and represents established knowledge about RCC incidence.

claims.claim: Translocation RCC comprises 20–75% of RCCs in childhood.
claims.source: Generally, RCCs are diagnosed in adults, with the exception of translocation RCC, which is driven by a hyper-activated fusion protein of the transcriptional activators TFE3 or TFEB and comprises 20–75% of RCCs in childhood (Ambalavanan and Geller, 2019; Caliò et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies and represents established knowledge about pediatric RCC.

claims.claim: Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome (BHD) is a dominantly inherited kidney cancer syndrome caused by mono-allelic germline loss-of-function mutations of the essential and conserved Folliculin (FLCN) gene.
claims.source: Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome (BHD) is a dominantly inherited kidney cancer syndrome caused by mono-allelic germline loss-of-function mutations of the essential and conserved Folliculin (FLCN) gene (Nahorski et al., 2011; Nickerson et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies and represents established knowledge about BHD syndrome etiology.

claims.claim: The lifetime risk for BHD patients to develop RCC is ~10 times higher than for the unaffected population.
claims.source: The lifetime risk for BHD patients to develop RCC is ~10 times higher than for the unaffected population (Houweling et al., 2011; Pavlovich et al., 2005; Toro et al., 2008; Zbar et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies and represents established knowledge about cancer risk in BHD patients.

claims.claim: BHD patients are predisposed to bilateral and multifocal renal tumors.
claims.source: BHD patients are predisposed to bilateral and multifocal renal tumors (Nickerson et al., 2002; Schmidt et al., 2005; Zbar et al., 2002) and dependent on surveillance by renal imaging for early detection and curative treatment prior to metastasis (Johannesma et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies and represents established knowledge about BHD tumor characteristics.

claims.claim: Loss of heterozygosity, by gene silencing or an inactivating somatic mutation of the wild-type FLCN allele, is a prerequisite for kidney cancer development in BHD patients.
claims.source: Loss of heterozygosity, by gene silencing or an inactivating somatic mutation of the wild-type FLCN allele, is a prerequisite for kidney cancer development in BHD patients (Vocke et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a genetic study and represents established knowledge about the two-hit hypothesis in BHD tumorigenesis.

claims.claim: FLCN has been connected to diverse cellular processes including mitochondrial biogenesis, stress resistance, autophagy, membrane trafficking, stem cell pluripotency, and ciliogenesis.
claims.source: These studies have connected FLCN to diverse cellular processes including mitochondrial biogenesis, stress resistance, autophagy, membrane trafficking, stem cell pluripotency, and ciliogenesis (Baba et al., 2006; Betschinger et al., 2013; Dunlop et al., 2014; Hasumi et al., 2012; Laviolette et al., 2013; Luijten et al., 2013; Nookala et al., 2012; Possik et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge about FLCN functions.

claims.claim: FLCN protein has been reported to affect multiple regulatory factors including mTOR, AMPK, HIF1, TGF-β, and Wnt.
claims.source: The FLCN protein has been reported to affect multiple regulatory factors including mTOR, AMPK, HIF1, TGF-β, and Wnt (Baba et al., 2006; De Zan et al., 2020; El-Houjeiri et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2010b; Khabibullin et al., 2014; Mathieu et al., 2019; Preston et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge about FLCN signaling connections.

claims.claim: The mechanism by which FLCN loss induces tumorigenesis is largely unknown.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the mechanism by which FLCN loss induces tumorigenesis is largely unknown.
claims.evidence: This represents a knowledge gap in the field and is supported by the conflicting results mentioned in the literature.

claims.claim: Conflicting results exist regarding activating or inhibitory effects of FLCN on mTOR signaling.
claims.source: Conflicting results, such as activating or inhibitory effects of FLCN on mTOR signaling (Baba et al., 2006; Bastola et al., 2013; Hartman et al., 2009; Hasumi et al., 2009; Hudon et al., 2010; Napolitano et al., 2020; Takagi et al., 2008; Tsun et al., 2013), and the range of the processes attributed to FLCN loss, prohibit a clear understanding of the pathways by which FLCN suppresses renal tumorigenesis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies with contradictory findings and represents a recognized problem in the field.

claims.claim: RPTEC/TERT1 cells retain the capacity to form 3D tubular structures.
claims.source: To study the effects of FLCN loss in a context relevant for oncogenesis, we used an immortalized, diploid renal proximal tubular epithelial cell line (RPTEC/TERT1, ATCC CRL-4031; Wieser et al., 2008, hereafter called RPTEC) as a model system, which retains the capacity to form 3D tubular structures (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating 3D tubular structure formation.

claims.claim: A TP53-dependent DNA damage response prohibits effective gene editing in some cell types.
claims.source: Because a TP53-dependent DNA damage response prohibits effective gene editing in some cell types (Haapaniemi et al., 2018; Ihry et al., 2018), we simultaneously knocked-out TP53 and FLCN to improve targeting efficiency.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge about CRISPR editing challenges.

claims.claim: Four out of six knock out (KO) cell lines had become aneuploid.
claims.source: By karyotypic analysis, we found that four out of six knock out (KO) cell lines had become aneuploid (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from karyotypic analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Aneuploidy occurred spontaneously during cell line formation because it appeared independently of FLCN, TP53, or inducible Cas9 status.
claims.source: We conclude, however, that aneuploidy occurred spontaneously during cell line formation because it appeared independently of FLCN, TP53, or inducible Cas9 status (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that aneuploidy did not correlate with specific genetic modifications.

claims.claim: Kidney tumors are often aneuploid.
claims.source: However, considering that kidney tumors are often aneuploid (Kardas et al., 2005; Morlote et al., 2019), we first used the cell lines of Figure 1D to identify FLCN-specific effects that occur independently of karyotype.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge about kidney tumor characteristics.

claims.claim: Expression of the renal proximal tubular marker aquaporin-1 (AQP1) was unchanged by FLCN and TP53 loss.
claims.source: Loss of FLCN and TP53 protein expression was confirmed by immunoblots, which also showed that expression of the renal proximal tubular marker aquaporin-1 (AQP1) was unchanged (Bedford et al., 2003; Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunoblots shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: FLCN prevents nuclear localization of TFE3 under nutrient-rich conditions.
claims.source: Previous studies reported that FLCN prevents nuclear localization of TFE3 under nutrient-rich conditions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge about FLCN-TFE3 regulation.

claims.claim: TFE3 and TFEB are transcription factors directing an autophagy and stress tolerance gene program under growth restrictive conditions.
claims.source: TFE3, and its close family member TFEB, are transcription factors directing an autophagy and stress tolerance gene program under growth restrictive conditions (Hong et al., 2010a; Wada et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge about TFE3/TFEB function.

claims.claim: RPTEC cells showed cytoplasmic TFE3 under normal growth conditions but TFE3 completely translocated to the nucleus after withdrawal of serum and amino acids.
claims.source: RPTEC cells showed cytoplasmic TFE3 under normal growth conditions but TFE3 completely translocated to the nucleus after withdrawal of serum and amino acids (Figure 1F, upper panels).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: TFE3 localized in the nucleus of the majority of cells from each of the three RPTEC FLCNNEG cell lines, independent of starvation or refeeding.
claims.source: In contrast, TFE3 localized in the nucleus of the majority of cells from each of the three RPTEC FLCNNEG cell lines, independent of starvation or refeeding, revealing that FLCNNEG cells fail to convey proper nutrient sensing and TFE3 responses (Figure 1F, lower panels and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: FLCNNEG cells fail to convey proper nutrient sensing and TFE3 responses.
claims.source: In contrast, TFE3 localized in the nucleus of the majority of cells from each of the three RPTEC FLCNNEG cell lines, independent of starvation or refeeding, revealing that FLCNNEG cells fail to convey proper nutrient sensing and TFE3 responses (Figure 1F, lower panels and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TFE3 localization does not respond to nutrient availability in FLCN knockout cells.

claims.claim: In the absence of FLCN, TFE3 is constitutively active in renal epithelial cells.
claims.source: We conclude that, in the absence of FLCN, TFE3 is constitutively active in renal epithelial cells, confirming TFE3 as a bona fide target of the FLCN tumor suppressor (El-Houjeiri et al., 2019; Wada et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing nuclear TFE3 localization and upregulation of TFE3 target genes, along with citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The majority of significantly altered genes was induced, rather than repressed, by FLCN inactivation.
claims.source: Interestingly, the majority of significantly altered genes was induced, rather than repressed, by FLCN inactivation: in FLCNNEG cells 426 genes were upregulated at least tenfold while only 62 genes were downregulated to the same extent (FDR < 0.05, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, lower panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: In FLCNNEG cells 426 genes were upregulated at least tenfold while only 62 genes were downregulated to the same extent.
claims.source: Interestingly, the majority of significantly altered genes was induced, rather than repressed, by FLCN inactivation: in FLCNNEG cells 426 genes were upregulated at least tenfold while only 62 genes were downregulated to the same extent (FDR < 0.05, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, lower panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics identified 5755 different proteins.
claims.source: To explore downstream consequences of FLCN loss at the protein level, we used mass spectrometry-based proteomics, identifying 5755 different proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis.

claims.claim: FLCN loss predominantly induced protein expression: 209 proteins were expressed at least fivefold higher in FLCNNEG cells, versus 41 proteins that were similarly downregulated.
claims.source: In concordance with our RNAseq data, FLCN loss predominantly induced protein expression: 209 proteins were expressed at least fivefold higher in FLCNNEG cells, versus 41 proteins that were similarly downregulated, out of a total of 914 differentially expressed proteins (p<0.05 and average count >1.5; Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, lower right).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from proteomic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claims.claim: Deletion of the transcriptional activator TP53 alone resulted in downregulation of gene expression.
claims.source: Conversely, as a control, deletion of the transcriptional activator TP53 alone (Farmer et al., 1992; Fields and Jang, 1990; Vogelstein and Kinzler, 1992) resulted in downregulation of gene expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, right, volcano plots of differential expression analysis by edgeR).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNAseq analysis and citations to previous studies about TP53 function.

claims.claim: Expression of differential RNAs showed variation between FLCNNEG RPTEC clones.
claims.source: Expression of differential RNAs showed variation between FLCNNEG RPTEC clones (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Hierarchical cluster analysis of differentially expressed proteins showed that replicates clustered together with a clear separation between the two groups.
claims.source: Nevertheless, hierarchical cluster analysis of differentially expressed proteins showed that replicates clustered together with a clear separation between the two groups (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), pointing to clonally independent effects of FLCN loss.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 2D, E.

claims.claim: FLCN is a powerful repressor of gene expression.
claims.source: Taken together, these results identify FLCN as a powerful repressor of gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that FLCN loss predominantly leads to gene upregulation.

claims.claim: A specific subset of 115 known TFE targets was upregulated in all three FLCNNEG cell lines.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found a specific subset of 115 known TFE targets to be upregulated in all three FLCNNEG cell lines (Figure 3A, cluster 3, boxed yellow, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from k-means Pearson correlation clustering of RNAseq data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Consistent upregulation of TFE target genes FNIP2, GPNMB, SQSTM1, RRAGC, GABARAP, ARHGAP12, AMDHD, WIPI1 and RRAGD was validated in all three FLCNNEG RPTEC clones using quantitative RT-PCR.
claims.source: Consistent upregulation of TFE target genes FNIP2, GPNMB, SQSTM1, RRAGC, GABARAP, ARHGAP12, AMDHD, WIPI1 and the more recently identified tumor growth-promoting TFE target RRAGD (not included in Figure 3A; Di Malta et al., 2017) was validated in all three FLCNNEG RPTEC clones using quantitative RT-PCR (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Western blots of GPNMB, RRAGD, SQSTM1, and FNIP2 showed these were strongly upregulated by FLCN inactivation, irrespective of TP53 status.
claims.source: Western blots of GPNMB, RRAGD, SQSTM1, and FNIP2, proteins associated with lysosome function, also showed these were strongly upregulated by FLCN inactivation, irrespective of TP53 status (Figure 3C; TP53wt FLCNKO refers to a TP53 positive FLCN knock out clone, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Western blots shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Induction of GPNMB, RRAGD, SQSTM1, FNIP2 and other E-box targets was significantly ameliorated in all three FLCNNEG RPTEC clones by simultaneously knocking down TFE3 and TFEB.
claims.source: Induction of GPNMB, RRAGD, SQSTM1, FNIP2 and other E-box targets was significantly ameliorated in all three FLCNNEG RPTEC clones by simultaneously knocking down TFE3 and its close family member TFEB (Figure 3D; siTFE3 only is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), an effect further confirmed in a TP53wt FLCNKO cell line shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR after siRNA knockdown shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: FLCN loss activates a specific category of TFE target genes in renal epithelial cells, independent of TP53 or karyotype.
claims.source: We conclude that FLCN loss activates a specific category of TFE target genes in renal epithelial cells, independent of TP53 or karyotype, many of which function in autophagy and lysosome regulation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing consistent upregulation of TFE targets across different clones with varying TP53 and karyotype status.

claims.claim: Many TFE target genes activated by FLCN loss function in autophagy and lysosome regulation.
claims.source: We conclude that FLCN loss activates a specific category of TFE target genes in renal epithelial cells, independent of TP53 or karyotype, many of which function in autophagy and lysosome regulation.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the functions of the identified TFE target genes.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation levels of 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase (S6K_T389) were not changed by FLCN loss in RPTECs.
claims.source: However, phosphorylation levels of two direct mTORC1 targets, 4E-BP1 (as judged by its electrophoretic mobility shift) and S6 kinase (S6K_T389) were not changed by FLCN loss in RPTECs, while also AKT/PKB_S437 phosphorylation remained intact (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Western blots shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: AKT/PKB_S437 phosphorylation remained intact after FLCN loss.
claims.source: However, phosphorylation levels of two direct mTORC1 targets, 4E-BP1 (as judged by its electrophoretic mobility shift) and S6 kinase (S6K_T389) were not changed by FLCN loss in RPTECs, while also AKT/PKB_S437 phosphorylation remained intact (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Western blots shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The dynamic subcellular localization of mTOR in response to starvation did not differ between FLCNPOS and FLCNNEG.
claims.source: The dynamic subcellular localization of mTOR in response to starvation did not differ between FLCNPOS and FLCNNEG as detected by immunofluorescent co-staining of mTOR and lysosomal marker LAMP2 (Figure 4B, FLCNNEG C3 is representative of the three FLCNNEG clones which all show normal mTOR dynamics).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: There is no evidence for directly altered mTOR signaling or nutrient sensing in the absence of FLCN in renal tubular cells.
claims.source: So, in contrast to several previous studies, but in line with a recent report (El-Houjeiri et al., 2019), we found no evidence for directly altered mTOR signaling or nutrient sensing in the absence of FLCN in renal tubular cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no changes in mTOR signaling markers and is consistent with one recent study.

claims.claim: Deletion of FLCN reduced proliferation of RPTEC cells significantly (p=8.31E-11).
claims.source: Growth curves confirmed that deletion of FLCN reduced proliferation of RPTEC cells significantly (p=8.31E-11; Table 1 and accompanying Figure in Materials and methods), an unexpected effect of tumor suppressor gene inactivation (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from growth curve measurements shown in Figure 5B and Table 1.

claims.claim: Reduced proliferation by FLCN loss is an unexpected effect of tumor suppressor gene inactivation.
claims.source: Growth curves confirmed that deletion of FLCN reduced proliferation of RPTEC cells significantly (p=8.31E-11; Table 1 and accompanying Figure in Materials and methods), an unexpected effect of tumor suppressor gene inactivation (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the expectation that tumor suppressor loss typically increases proliferation.

claims.claim: In FLCNNEG RPTECs, the immune-response-related hallmarks were highly significantly enriched in both RNA and protein data.
claims.source: Interestingly, however, in FLCNNEG RPTECs, the immune-response-related hallmarks were highly significantly enriched in both RNA and protein data (Figure 5A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, IFN_GAMMA_RESPONSE, IFN_ALPHA_RESPONSE, COMPLEMENT).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: BinGO gene ontology analyses of differential expression patterns in FLCNNEG RPTECs revealed many overlapping immune and IFN response signature genes, including ISG15, IFIT1, IF16, MX1, OAS2, and STAT2 in both RNA and protein data.
claims.source: BinGO (Maere et al., 2005) gene ontology analyses of differential expression patterns in FLCNNEG RPTECs also revealed many overlapping immune and IFN response signature genes, including ISG15, IFIT1, IF16, MX1, OAS2, and STAT2 in both RNA and protein data (Figure 5C,D; orange circles show overlap).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5C and D.

claims.claim: The IFN response signature program is a key target of FLCN in renal epithelial cells.
claims.source: These findings indicate that the IFN response signature program is a key target of FLCN in renal epithelial cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the strong enrichment of IFN response genes in FLCN knockout cells.

claims.claim: The majority of regulatory elements enriched in FLCNNEG RPTEC can be assigned to either the basic helix-loop-helix E-box motif group or to the Interferon-Stimulated Response Element (ISRE) motif group.
claims.source: Importantly, the majority of regulatory elements enriched in FLCNNEG RPTEC can be assigned to either the basic helix-loop-helix E-box motif group (e.g. regulated by TFE3/TFEB) or to the Interferon-Stimulated Response Element (ISRE) motif group (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from iRegulon analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Significant induction of the ISRE targets MX1, ISG15, IRF9, IFIT1, STAT1, and STAT2 next to TFE3 and E-box targets GPNMB, RRAGD, FNIP2, CTSD, and SQSTM1 were validated by qPCR.
claims.source: Significant induction of the ISRE targets MX1, ISG15, IRF9, IFIT1, STAT1, and STAT2 next to TFE3 and E-box targets GPNMB, RRAGD, FNIP2, CTSD, and SQSTM1 were validated by qPCR in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from qPCR shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Elevated expression of both the ISRE and E-box associated genes was observed in FLCNNEG BHD tumors.
claims.source: Although full interpretation of these results awaits the analysis of a larger tumor sample size, we observed elevated expression of both the ISRE as E-box associated genes in FLCNNEG BHD tumors (Figure 6I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from proteomic analysis of BHD tumors shown in Figure 6I, though the sample size is limited.

claims.claim: FLCN loss upregulates two major gene classes: TFE3/TFEB regulated E-box targets and IFN-associated ISRE targets.
claims.source: Based on these results, we conclude that FLCN loss upregulates two major gene classes: TFE3/TFEB regulated E-box targets and IFN-associated ISRE targets.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNAseq, proteomics, and iRegulon analysis.

claims.claim: These genes and their protein products are candidate positive biomarkers for FLCN loss in BHD-related kidney cancer.
claims.source: Our integrated analysis reveals these genes and their protein products as candidate positive biomarkers for FLCN loss in BHD-related kidney cancer.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the consistent upregulation of these genes in FLCN knockout cells and preliminary tumor data.

claims.claim: FLCN acts in a protein complex with FNIP1 and FNIP2.
claims.source: FLCN acts in a protein complex with FNIP1 and FNIP2 (Baba et al., 2006; Hasumi et al., 2015; Hasumi et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge about FLCN protein interactions.

claims.claim: When FNIP1 and FNIP2 are inactivated simultaneously, mice develop kidney cancer.
claims.source: When FNIP1 and FNIP2 are inactivated simultaneously, mice develop kidney cancer (Hasumi et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and represents established knowledge from mouse models.

claims.claim: Upregulation of ISRE or E-box motif genes is specifically connected to inactivation of the FLCN-FNIP1/FNIP2 axis.
claims.source: This confirmed that upregulation of ISRE or E-box motif genes is specifically connected to inactivation of the FLCN-FNIP1/FNIP2 axis (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR in FNIP1/2 knockout cells shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: TFE3 localized to the nucleus upon FNIP1/2 loss.
claims.source: Furthermore, TFE3 localized to the nucleus upon FNIP1/2 loss (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: ISRE and E-box associated genes were not induced in RPE1 cells by FLCN loss.
claims.source: Quantitative RT-PCR analyses revealed that, strikingly, ISRE and E-box associated genes were not induced in RPE1 cells by FLCN loss (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR in FLCN knockout RPE1 cells shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: RRAGD was the only exception yet was induced ~10 times less strongly in RPE1 as compared to RPTEC cells.
claims.source: RRAGD was the only exception yet was induced ~10 times less strongly in RPE1 as compared to RPTEC cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR comparing RPE1 and RPTEC cells.

claims.claim: The two main gene induction programs directed by FLCN-FNIP1/2 are renal specific.
claims.source: These results indicate that the two main gene induction programs directed by FLCN-FNIP1/2 are renal specific.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these programs are not activated in RPE1 cells.

claims.claim: iRegulon analysis of differential RNAs overlapping with differential proteins upon FLCN loss predicted STAT1 and STAT2-binding motifs as the most enriched upstream regulatory elements.
claims.source: Upon selecting the most significantly overlapping effects (FDR < 0.01, n = 181) (Figure 7C), iRegulon analysis of differential RNAs overlapping with differential proteins (r > 0.8, n = 49) upon FLCN loss predicted STAT1 and STAT2-binding motifs as the most enriched upstream regulatory elements (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from iRegulon analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: FLCN re-expression in FLCNNEG RPTEC C2 restored regulation of TFE3 localization and nutrient sensing.
claims.source: FLCN re-expression in FLCNNEG RPTEC C2 restored regulation of TFE3 localization and nutrient sensing (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Re-introducing FLCN completely reverted the ISRE expression phenotype.
claims.source: Moreover, re-introducing FLCN completely reverted the ISRE expression phenotype (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR after FLCN re-expression shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Upregulation of the ISRE-associated gene program was entirely STAT1/2-dependent.
claims.source: Quantitative RT-PCR showed that upregulation of the ISRE-associated gene program was entirely STAT1/2-dependent (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR after STAT1/2 knockdown shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Immunoblotting subcellular fractions showed higher protein levels of both STAT1 and STAT2 in FLCNNEG cells.
claims.source: In addition, immunoblotting subcellular fractions showed higher protein levels of both STAT1 and STAT2 in FLCNNEG cells (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Western blots of subcellular fractions shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: Nuclear STAT2 was exclusively bound to chromatin in the absence of FLCN.
claims.source: Importantly, nuclear STAT2 was exclusively bound to chromatin in the absence of FLCN (Figure 7G) identifying STAT2 as a key target of FLCN.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from chromatin fractionation shown in Figure 7G.

claims.claim: STAT2 is a key target of FLCN.
claims.source: Importantly, nuclear STAT2 was exclusively bound to chromatin in the absence of FLCN (Figure 7G) identifying STAT2 as a key target of FLCN.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that STAT2 chromatin binding is specifically enhanced by FLCN loss.

claims.claim: No secreted IFNγ or IFNα was detected in FLCNNEG RPTEC cell lines.
claims.source: However, we did not detect any secreted IFNγ or IFNα, indicating that autocrine stimulation of IFN signaling did not cause the upregulated ISRE gene program or chromatin binding of STAT2 in FLCNNEG RPTEC (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from CBA and ELISA measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Autocrine stimulation of IFN signaling did not cause the upregulated ISRE gene program or chromatin binding of STAT2 in FLCNNEG RPTEC.
claims.source: However, we did not detect any secreted IFNγ or IFNα, indicating that autocrine stimulation of IFN signaling did not cause the upregulated ISRE gene program or chromatin binding of STAT2 in FLCNNEG RPTEC (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of detectable IFN secretion.

claims.claim: IFNA, IFNB and IFNG expression was not detected in FLCNNEG RPTEC.
claims.source: Also, we did not detect IFNA, IFNB and IFNG expression, nor differential expression of the IFN receptors (IFNAR1, IFNAR2, IFNGR1 and IFNGR2) in FLCNNEG RPTEC (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: There was no differential expression of the IFN receptors (IFNAR1, IFNAR2, IFNGR1 and IFNGR2) in FLCNNEG RPTEC.

results.result: FLCN loss causes constitutive nuclear localization of TFE3 in renal epithelial cells, independent of nutrient availability. This effect is reversible upon FLCN re-expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C30-C33 demonstrate nuclear TFE3 localization in FLCN knockout cells under all nutrient conditions using immunofluorescence (Figure 1F). Claim C70 shows rescue by FLCN re-expression (Figure 7—supplement 1E). The data are consistent across multiple clones and include appropriate controls (starvation/refeeding conditions).

results.result: FLCN loss upregulates a specific subset of 115 TFE3/TFEB E-box target genes involved in autophagy and lysosome regulation, including GPNMB, RRAGD, SQSTM1, and FNIP2. This upregulation is TFE3/TFEB-dependent and independent of TP53 status or karyotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 provide convergent evidence from RNAseq (Figure 3A), qRT-PCR (Figure 3B), and Western blot (Figure 3C) across multiple independent clones. Claim C45 demonstrates TFE3/TFEB dependency through siRNA knockdown (Figure 3D). The consistency across different genetic backgrounds (TP53+/-, aneuploid/diploid) strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: FLCN loss does not alter mTORC1 signaling in RPTEC cells, as evidenced by unchanged phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 and S6K, normal AKT phosphorylation, and normal mTOR subcellular localization dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 provide multiple lines of evidence (Western blots in Figure 4A, immunofluorescence in Figure 4B) showing no changes in canonical mTORC1 signaling markers. This contradicts some previous studies but aligns with recent work (El-Houjeiri et al., 2019). The data are clear and reproducible across three independent experiments.

results.result: FLCN loss induces interferon response genes independently of interferon, with enrichment of ISRE motif-containing genes including ISG15, IFIT1, MX1, OAS2, and STAT2 in both RNA and protein datasets.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 demonstrate IFN response gene enrichment through GSEA (Figure 5A), gene ontology analysis (Figure 5C-D), and iRegulon motif analysis (Figure 6D). Claim C6 is validated by qPCR (Figure 6—supplement 1C). The convergence of transcriptomic and proteomic data strengthens this finding. However, the mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: FLCN loss promotes STAT2 recruitment to chromatin and upregulation of ISRE genes through a non-canonical, IFN-independent mechanism involving unphosphorylated STAT1 and STAT2, without activation of canonical IFN receptor signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 demonstrate STAT1/2 dependency (siRNA knockdown, Figure 7E), increased STAT1/2 protein levels (Figure 7F), and enhanced STAT2 chromatin binding (Figure 7G). Claims C76-C81 rule out canonical IFN signaling through multiple negative results (no IFN secretion, no receptor expression changes, no JAK/TYK phosphorylation, no STAT1 phosphorylation). The evidence is comprehensive, though the mechanism remains incompletely understood.

results.result: FLCN loss significantly reduces cellular proliferation in RPTEC cells (p=8.31E-11), an effect that is reversible upon FLCN re-expression and occurs regardless of TP53 status.
results.evaluation: Claims C52 and C8 report statistically significant growth reduction with appropriate p-value (8.31E-11) from growth curve modeling (Figure 5B, Table 1). Claim C87 demonstrates rescue by FLCN re-expression (Figure 8D). Claims C86 shows consistency across TP53 backgrounds. The statistical analysis using random intercept modeling is appropriate and rigorous.

results.result: FLCN loss dominantly suppresses the hyperproliferative effects of oncogenic SFPQ-TFE3 fusion protein, reducing proliferation to levels similar to IFNγ treatment, demonstrating that STAT2-mediated growth inhibition counteracts TFE3-driven proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 show that FLCN knockout in SFPQ-TFE3 cells reduces proliferation (Figure 8C, 8E) and correlates with ISRE gene induction (Figure 8—supplement 1D). Claim C103 demonstrates that TFE3 activation alone promotes hyperproliferation. Claim C104 shows equivalence to IFNγ treatment. The experimental design directly tests the interaction between TFE3 and STAT2 pathways.

results.result: The FLCN-FNIP1/2 protein complex specifically regulates both E-box and ISRE gene programs in a renal-specific manner, as demonstrated by similar effects in FNIP1/2 double knockout cells and absence of these effects in RPE1 cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 shows FNIP1/2 knockout recapitulates FLCN knockout effects (Figure 7A), and C65 shows nuclear TFE3 localization (Figure 7—supplement 1B). Claim C68 demonstrates tissue specificity by showing no induction in RPE1 cells (Figure 7B). The comparison across cell types is appropriate, though limited to two cell lines.

results.result: The TFE3 and STAT1/2 gene activation programs are independent effects of FLCN loss, as TFE3 activation alone (SFPQ-TFE3) does not induce ISRE genes or STAT2 chromatin binding, and STAT1/2 knockdown does not affect E-box genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 show SFPQ-TFE3 expression induces E-box but not ISRE genes (Figure 8A) and does not recruit STAT2 to chromatin (Figure 8B). Claims C118-C120 demonstrate reciprocal independence through siRNA experiments (Figure 7E). The bidirectional testing strengthens the conclusion of pathway independence.

results.result: Both ISRE and E-box associated genes show elevated expression in BHD tumors, suggesting these genes may serve as biomarkers for FLCN loss in BHD-related kidney cancer.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 reports elevated expression in BHD tumors (Figure 6I), but explicitly acknowledges limited sample size (n=2 tumors). Claim C111 mentions immune cell presence at tumor margins (unpublished). The biomarker potential (C61) is speculative. The tumor validation is insufficient for strong conclusions and requires analysis of larger cohorts.

results.result: FLCN functions as a powerful repressor of gene expression, with FLCN loss predominantly inducing rather than repressing gene expression (426 genes upregulated ≥10-fold vs. 62 downregulated at RNA level; 209 proteins upregulated ≥5-fold vs. 41 downregulated).
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 provide specific quantification from RNAseq (Figure 2—supplement 1D), and C37 from proteomics (Figure 2—supplement 2E). The convergence of RNA and protein data supports the conclusion. Claim C41 is a reasonable inference. Statistical thresholds (FDR<0.05 for RNA, p<0.05 for protein) are appropriate.

results.result: Four out of six knockout cell lines became aneuploid during cell line generation, occurring spontaneously and independently of FLCN, TP53, or Cas9 status, consistent with the known aneuploidy of kidney tumors.
results.evaluation: Claim C24 reports karyotypic analysis results (Figure 1D). Claim C25 provides a reasonable inference about spontaneous occurrence based on lack of correlation with genetic modifications. Claim C26 provides context from literature. The authors appropriately address this confounding factor by using multiple clones and later generating diploid lines.

results.result: Despite variation in differential RNA expression between FLCN knockout clones, hierarchical clustering of differentially expressed proteins shows clear separation between FLCN-positive and FLCN-negative groups, indicating clonally independent effects.
results.evaluation: Claim C39 acknowledges clone-to-clone variation (Figure 2D), while C40 shows that protein-level clustering is robust (Figure 2D-E, Figure 2—supplement 2D). The proteomic data provide stronger evidence for FLCN-specific effects than RNA alone. This addresses potential concerns about clonal artifacts.

results.result: iRegulon analysis of genes showing high correlation between RNA and protein changes identifies STAT1 and STAT2-binding motifs as the most enriched regulatory elements, and FLCN re-expression completely reverts the ISRE expression phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claim C69 describes computational analysis with appropriate filtering (FDR<0.01, r>0.8) shown in Figure 7C-D. Claim C71 provides functional validation through rescue experiments (Figure 7E). The integration of computational prediction and experimental validation is methodologically sound.

results.result: While FLCN loss clearly promotes STAT2 chromatin binding, the mechanism remains unresolved. FLCN does not directly bind STAT2, and STAT2 protein stability and nucleo-cytoplasmic distribution are unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 acknowledge the knowledge gap. Claims C121-C123 report negative results from mechanistic experiments (unpublished data mentioned in text). This honest acknowledgment of limitations is appropriate. The result identifies an important area for future investigation.

results.result: GPNMB, RRAGD, ASAH1, and FNIP2 are strongly upregulated by FLCN loss, with FNIP2 upregulation representing a potential feedback mechanism. GPNMB and RRAGD show particular promise as biomarkers for FLCN inactivation.
results.evaluation: Claim C124 reports consistent upregulation across multiple assays. Claim C125 provides a reasonable inference about FNIP2 feedback. Claim C126 shows similar effects in FNIP1/2 knockout cells. Claim C127 is speculative but based on strong and consistent data. The biomarker potential requires clinical validation.

results.result: The RPTEC/TERT1 cell line retains key characteristics of renal proximal tubular epithelial cells, including capacity to form 3D tubular structures and expression of the proximal tubular marker AQP1.
results.evaluation: Claim C22 is demonstrated by imaging (Figure 1A), and C27 by Western blot (Figure 1E). These validation experiments establish the appropriateness of the cell model. However, the work relies heavily on this single cell line, which is a limitation.

results.result: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics identified 5,755 proteins, and as a control, TP53 deletion alone resulted in downregulation of gene expression, contrasting with FLCN loss.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 reports the proteomic coverage (Figure 2—supplement 2C, E). Claim C38 provides an important control showing opposite effects of TP53 deletion (Figure 2—supplement 1E), validating that FLCN's role as a transcriptional repressor is specific and not a general artifact.

results.result: Loss of FLCN in RPTEC/TERT1 cells has three main effects: reduced proliferation, TFE3 activation with E-box gene upregulation, and IFN-independent STAT2 activation with ISRE gene upregulation. These effects are renal-specific and reversible by FLCN re-expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 summarize the main findings with appropriate integration of multiple lines of evidence. The three main effects are each well-supported by the data. The renal specificity (C101) is demonstrated by RPE1 comparison, and reversibility (C102) by rescue experiments. This represents a comprehensive summary of the work.

results.result: The authors propose that STAT1/2 activation counterbalances TFE3-driven hyperproliferation and may form a barrier to tumorigenesis, though STAT2 activation could alternatively contribute to pro-oncogenic inflammation. BHD tumors may fall into two classes based on IFN signature levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C105-C107, C112-C113, and C115 are largely speculative interpretations based on the experimental findings. While the growth inhibition data (C10, C105) are solid, the implications for tumorigenesis (C106, C112-C113) and tumor classification (C115) are hypothetical. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future testing but lack direct experimental support.

results.result: GPNMB is frequently upregulated in various tumors including renal cancer, though its tumorigenic role is unclear. GPNMB can be targeted by antibody-drug conjugates like glembatumumab vedotin, providing a potential therapeutic approach for BHD tumors.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129 cite established knowledge about GPNMB. Claim C130 cites clinical trials for GPNMB-targeted therapy. Claim C131 is speculative about application to BHD tumors. While the therapeutic potential is interesting, it requires validation in BHD-specific contexts. The suggestion is reasonable but preliminary.

results.result: Recent work shows TFEB is the main driver of kidney abnormalities in BHD mouse models through mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation involving Rag GTPases. Despite upregulation of RagC and RagD in the current study, no mTORC1 hyperactivation was observed, suggesting potential species differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C135 cite recent literature (Napolitano et al., 2020). Claim C136 reports the authors' negative findings for mTORC1 activation. Claims C137-C138 offer speculative explanations for the discrepancy. The acknowledgment of conflicting results and potential species differences is scientifically appropriate, though the speculation is not directly tested.

results.result: Several genes were downregulated by FLCN loss, showing overlapping biological processes in GSEA analysis, but iRegulon analysis failed to identify a common upstream transcriptional regulator.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C140 report negative results from computational analyses. The honest reporting of failed attempts to identify regulatory mechanisms for downregulated genes is appropriate. This represents an incomplete aspect of the work that requires further investigation.

results.result: Background claims establishing the clinical and molecular context of BHD syndrome, FLCN function, and related kidney cancers, including the knowledge gap about FLCN's mechanism in tumorigenesis.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C2, C12-C21, C23, C26, C28-C29, C62-C63, C94-C98, C108, C114, C132) represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited. They provide necessary context for the study. The citations appear accurate and relevant. Claim C20 appropriately identifies the knowledge gap that motivates the current work.

results.result: The authors identify STAT1/2 signaling as a novel target of FLCN and suggest it may influence immune responses, though the connection to inflammation in renal cells is unclear. The findings may facilitate biomarker discovery and therapeutic strategies for BHD patients.
results.evaluation: Claim C9 is well-supported by the data. Claims C11, C92-C93 are speculative about immune/inflammatory roles. Claims C109-C110 report negative results for inflammatory cytokines, suggesting the IFN program may not be inflammatory in renal cells. Claims C141-C142 are speculative about translational applications. The speculation is reasonable but requires substantial additional work.
